Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Views and Reusable S Q L Objects in Postgres
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 12, Views and Reusable S Q L Objects in Postgres.

In Module 11, you learned how to organize advanced queries with common table expressions and window functions. Those tools are useful inside one analysis. But what happens when the same trusted logic is needed by many reports, many analysts, or many applications?

[tts-break]

That is where this module begins. We are moving from writing one good query to creating reusable database interfaces.

We will start with standard views. Then we will look at materialized views, which store a snapshot of a query result. We will also discuss dependencies, updates through views, access boundaries, and freshness.

The main question to keep in mind is simple: which logic should stay inside one query, and which logic is stable enough to become a reusable database object?

slides.title: Why views matter
slides.transcript:
Views matter because they let us define important logic once and reuse it.

Suppose five reports all need the same patient and admission join. We could copy that join into five different queries. But if the logic changes later, we now have five places to update.

A view gives that shared logic one name and one definition. Reports can query the view instead of rebuilding the same steps.

A view can also expose only the columns that are useful for a task. That can reduce accidental exposure, but permissions still need to be configured separately.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript:
By the end of this module, you should be able to create and use standard views, inspect how they are defined, and understand what other objects they depend on.

You should also be able to explain when a simple view can accept updates, what the with check option does, and why a materialized view can become stale.

Most importantly, you should be able to choose among three tools: a common table expression for logic used inside one statement, a standard view for shared live logic, and a materialized view for a stored result that can be refreshed.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript:
We will start with modularity and standard views.

[tts-break]

Then we will inspect reusable objects and their dependencies. After that, we will explore controlled writes and access boundaries.

Materialized views come next, with a focus on freshness and refresh policy. Finally, we will combine views and common table expressions into a small reusable analytics layer.

slides.title: Teaching database
slides.transcript:
The database contains a few small source areas. Patient and admission tables support healthcare-style views. Employee, department, and sales-order tables support a performance interface.

Customer transactions support recent activity and retention examples. Reusable objects are placed in an analytics schema so the source tables and analytical interfaces are clearly separated.

slides.title: Modular architecture
slides.transcript:
Modularity works best when each layer has one responsibility.

[tts-break]

Base tables store source facts. A shared view can own stable relational logic.

A report-level common table expression can own a temporary threshold, ranking rule, or sequence calculation. The final query produces the consumer-specific result. This separation makes each layer easier to test and change.

slides.title: Three reusable choices
slides.transcript:
We have three main choices for reusable query logic.

A common table expression exists only while one S Q L statement is running. It is useful for organizing temporary stages inside that statement.

A standard view is saved in the database, but it stores the query definition rather than a separate copy of the result.

A materialized view is also saved in the database, but it stores the result itself.

The choice depends on three questions: how often the logic will be reused, how current the result must be, and how expensive the underlying query is.

slides.title: What a standard view stores
slides.transcript:
A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate snapshot of the rows.

Here is a simple way to think about it. Imagine a window looking into the underlying tables. The window has a name, and the view definition controls what you can see through it.

[tts-break]

When the source tables change, the next query against the view uses the current source data. We do not have to manually refresh a standard view.

So a standard view is useful when we want reusable logic and current data at the same time.

slides.title: View contract
slides.transcript:
Think of a view as a contract between the database and the people who use it.

The contract includes the object name, the exposed columns, the data types, and the meaning of one row. That last part is the grain.

For example, if a view promises one row per admission, changing it later to one row per patient is not a small change. The query might still run, but the meaning of the data has changed.

Shared views should therefore be changed carefully, just like an interface in software.

slides.title: Explore database objects
slides.transcript:
Run the schema exploration query first.

Look at objects in the public and analytics schemas. The public schema contains source tables.

The analytics schema contains reusable interfaces. This separation is helpful because object location can communicate purpose.

slides.title: Query a view
slides.transcript:
This query reads the patient admission summary view.

Consumers do not need to repeat the join or stay-duration expression. The view already defines that interface.

Run it and identify the grain. One row represents one admission with selected patient attributes and a derived stay duration.

slides.title: Create a view
slides.transcript:
Before creating a view, make four decisions.

Choose a meaningful name. Define the row grain.

Choose the columns intentionally. Then write the select statement that implements that interface. Starting with the contract makes the S Q L easier to evaluate.

slides.title: Create or Replace View
slides.transcript:
The create or replace view command lets us change a compatible view definition without dropping the view first.

That sounds convenient, and it is. But do not confuse a successful command with a safe change.

If we rename a column, change a data type, or change what one row represents, downstream reports may behave differently even when the database accepts the new definition.

So after changing a shared view, review the contract: name, columns, types, and grain.

slides.title: Use the view for aggregation
slides.transcript:
Once the patient admission interface exists, later reports can start from it.

This query groups the reusable admission rows by department.

The report author does not need to repeat patient joins or stay-duration calculations. That is the value of modular S Q L. stable logic is centralized, and consumer queries become smaller.

slides.title: Naming conventions
slides.transcript:
This course uses V W as a prefix for standard views and M V for materialized views. Postgres does not require that naming convention.

The goal is readability and discoverability. Whatever convention a team chooses, use it consistently and document the intended grain and meaning of important shared objects.

slides.title: Inspect view definitions
slides.transcript:
Shared database objects should not be mysterious. the Postgres information schema can show view names and definitions.

Run this query and inspect the S Q L behind the analytics views. Being able to inspect a view helps with debugging, documentation, and change review.

slides.title: Inspect dependencies
slides.transcript:
A shared view depends on other database objects.

[tts-break]

This query uses information schema metadata to show which tables feed each view.

Dependency awareness matters because changing a base object or shared view can affect several downstream consumers. Before making a breaking change, understand the dependency chain.

slides.title: Dependency chain
slides.transcript:
A reusable view can sit in the middle of a larger dependency chain.

Base tables feed the view. A report may then query that view directly, or a common table expression may use the view as its starting point. A dashboard or application may depend on the final result.

[tts-break]

This means one change near the beginning can affect several downstream objects.

Before making a breaking change, ask: what uses this view, and what assumptions do those users make about it?

slides.title: Change management
slides.transcript:
Change management goes beyond syntax.

A create or replace command may succeed, but a meaningful change can still break analytics.

Consumers may depend on a column name, data type, business definition, or row grain. Review those contract elements before changing a shared object.

slides.title: Simple views can be updatable
slides.transcript:
Some simple views can be updated directly.

If a view is based on one table and keeps a clear one to one relationship with the underlying rows, Postgres may allow an update through the view to change the base table.

But this does not apply to every view. A view with joins, grouping, or aggregate calculations may not have a clear single source row to update.

So treat write behavior as something you verify, not something you assume.

slides.title: Update through a view
slides.transcript:
This example updates the city value through a simple view.

The returning clause immediately shows the row that would be changed. Then the transaction is rolled back, so the teaching database returns to its original state.

This is a useful testing pattern. Make the change inside a transaction, inspect what happened, and keep or undo the change only after you understand the result.

slides.title: Filtered updatable view
slides.transcript:
A filtered view creates an interesting question about updates.

Suppose the view shows only active patients. Now imagine we update one of those patients through the view and set active to false.

Without additional protection, the update may succeed. The row then disappears from the view because it no longer satisfies the filter.

The with check option lets us prevent that kind of update when we want the row to remain valid according to the view's own condition.

slides.title: With Check Option
slides.transcript:
The with check option enforces the view condition when someone writes through the view.

If the view shows only active patients, an update through that view must still produce an active patient. If the update would make the row fall outside the view, Postgres rejects it.

This gives the view a more controlled write behavior. It is useful, but it does not replace normal constraints, permissions, or other database rules.

slides.title: Check Option failure
slides.transcript:
This example intentionally fails.

The active-patient view shows only active rows and includes a check option. The update tries to set an active patient to inactive through that view.

Because the resulting row would no longer satisfy the view condition, Postgres rejects the update. This is expected behavior.

slides.title: Do not infer writability
slides.transcript:
Do not assume every view is writable.

A simple single table view may support automatic updates. A join or aggregate view does not have the same direct row mapping.

Materialized views are stored query results, not ordinary write through interfaces. Always check the actual Postgres behavior for the view definition you are designing.

slides.title: Views as access boundaries
slides.transcript:
Views can also create a narrower interface for analytics.

For example, an analyst may need age group, city, and activity status, but not the patient's name, email address, or date of birth. A view can expose only the fields needed for that task.

[tts-break]

That can reduce accidental exposure, but it is important to use precise language. Hiding a column in a view does not automatically prevent someone from querying the base table.

Real access control still depends on permissions, roles, and sometimes row level security.

slides.title: Limited analytics view
slides.transcript:
This analytics view exposes subject I D, age band, city, and active status.

It omits name, email, and date of birth. That creates a narrower analytical interface.

Run it and compare the result with the source patient table. The design reduces unnecessary fields, but access to objects must still be configured separately.

slides.title: Security Invoker
slides.transcript:
Postgres also supports a setting called security invoker for views.

With this setting, Postgres checks access to the underlying tables using the permissions of the person who is running the view.

This matters in real systems with multiple roles and permission levels.

For this course, focus on the idea: the view definition and the permission model are connected, and both need to be tested in the environment where the view will actually be used.

slides.title: Security Invoker S Q L
slides.transcript:
This query recreates the patient analytics view with security invoker enabled.

It still exposes the same selected analytical columns.

The key difference is how Postgres evaluates underlying access permissions. In a production environment, you would test this with real roles and grants.

slides.title: Security boundaries
slides.transcript:
Views are useful security-adjacent interfaces, but they should not be described as secure or compliant simply because they hide columns.

[tts-break]

Permissions still matter. Row-level security may matter.

Application access paths matter. Compliance depends on a broader system of controls. Keep the claim proportional to what the view actually does.

slides.title: Materialized views
slides.transcript:
A materialized view is different from a standard view because it stores the query result.

Think of it as a prepared snapshot. Suppose a dashboard needs the same expensive summary again and again. Instead of recalculating the summary every time, we can store the result in a materialized view.

[tts-break]

That can make repeated reads faster. But now we have a new responsibility: the stored snapshot can become old.

So whenever you use a materialized view, you must think about both performance and freshness.

slides.title: When materialization helps
slides.transcript:
A materialized view is useful when the same expensive summary is needed repeatedly and users can accept some delay between the source data and the stored result.

For example, a dashboard may not need second by second updates. A snapshot refreshed every hour may be completely acceptable.

But the refresh policy has to be clear. Users should know when the snapshot was last refreshed and what happens if a refresh fails.

slides.title: Create materialized view
slides.transcript:
This example creates a diagnosis summary as a materialized view.

One row represents one diagnosis. The stored measures include the number of admissions, the number of distinct patients, and the average length of stay.

The example also stores a refresh time so we can see when the snapshot was generated.

That refresh time does not change simply because someone queries the materialized view. It changes when the stored result is rebuilt.

slides.title: Materialized view grain
slides.transcript:
Materialized views still need a clear grain.

In this example, one row represents one diagnosis. The measures summarize admissions for that diagnosis.

The refresh time value records when the stored result was produced. Consumers need both the grain and freshness information to interpret the data correctly.

slides.title: Query the snapshot
slides.transcript:
Once the materialized view exists, consumers can query the stored summary directly.

The report query is simple because the aggregation has already been computed.

But remember that the result is only as fresh as the last successful refresh.

slides.title: Freshness timeline
slides.transcript:
Freshness is easiest to understand with a timeline.

Imagine the materialized view is refreshed at nine in the morning. At ten, a new admission is inserted into the source table. A normal query against the source can see that new row immediately.

The materialized view cannot see it yet because its stored snapshot still represents nine o'clock.

[tts-break]

After the materialized view is refreshed again, the snapshot catches up.

That time difference between the source and the snapshot is not automatically a problem. It becomes a problem only when users expect fresher data than the system is designed to provide.

slides.title: Create stale snapshot demo
slides.transcript:
This example inserts another Influenza admission into the base table.

Then it compares the live base-table count with the stored materialized view count. The base table changes immediately.

The snapshot remains unchanged because it has not been refreshed. This demonstrates staleness directly.

slides.title: Refresh materialized view
slides.transcript:
Refreshing a materialized view rebuilds the stored result from its underlying query.

In this example, after we create a stale condition, we refresh the materialized view and compare the counts again.

The stored diagnosis count should now match the current source data, and the refresh time should show when the new snapshot was created.

slides.title: Freshness is a contract
slides.transcript:
Freshness is part of the data contract.

Users should know how often the snapshot is refreshed, when the last successful refresh occurred, and how much delay is acceptable.

They should also know what happens when a refresh fails.

A materialized view without a clear freshness policy can be technically correct but operationally confusing.

slides.title: Index a materialized view
slides.transcript:
Because a materialized view stores rows, Postgres can index those rows.

[tts-break]

This example creates a unique index on diagnosis.

Indexes may support faster reads and are also relevant to certain Postgres concurrent refresh requirements. Choose indexes based on real query patterns and constraints, not simply because the object is materialized.

slides.title: Concurrent refresh note
slides.transcript:
Production Postgres supports refresh materialized view concurrently under specific conditions.

An appropriate unique index is required.

Concurrent refresh is an availability technique. It does not remove the need for a refresh policy, freshness metadata, or monitoring.

slides.title: Compare live and snapshot
slides.transcript:
A useful monitoring pattern is to compare the live result with the stored snapshot.

This query shows diagnosis counts from both sources.

After a successful refresh, the values should agree for the same logic. If they differ unexpectedly, investigate whether the snapshot is stale or the definitions are inconsistent.

slides.title: Common Table Expression versus view versus materialized view
slides.transcript:
Here is a simple decision rule for choosing among these objects.

If the logic is needed only inside one query, a common table expression is usually enough.

If many queries need the same reusable logic and they should always read current source data, use a standard view.

[tts-break]

If many queries need the same expensive summary, and some delay is acceptable, a materialized view may be a better choice.

The best object is not the most advanced one. It is the one that matches the reuse, freshness, and performance requirements.

slides.title: Promote only stable logic
slides.transcript:
A useful architecture rule is to promote stable meaning into persistent objects.

If many consumers agree on what a patient admission row means, that can become a view. If one report uses a temporary thirty day threshold, keep that logic in the report.

If a summary is expensive and reused frequently, materialization may be appropriate. Do not turn every query into a database object.

slides.title: View + Common Table Expression
slides.transcript:
This example combines ideas from Modules 11 and 12.

The standard view owns the stable patient admission logic. A common table expression then adds report specific sequence logic.

The lag function, which gives us the previous value, retrieves the earlier discharge time. The report then checks whether the next admission happened within thirty days.

[tts-break]

This is good modular design because stable shared meaning stays in the view, while a temporary analytical rule stays in the report.

slides.title: Project architecture
slides.transcript:
The project asks you to design a small analytics layer for three different needs.

Employee performance is stable shared logic, so a standard view makes sense.

Recent customer activity can also be a reusable view, while a specific inactivity threshold can stay in a common table expression because different reports may use different thresholds.

The diagnosis dashboard uses a repeatedly requested summary, so a materialized view can make sense when a known refresh delay is acceptable.

slides.title: Employee performance view
slides.transcript:
This view joins employees to departments and sales orders.

It aggregates orders and sales amount.

One output row represents one employee. Because this definition can support several operations reports, publishing it as a reusable view is reasonable.

slides.title: Consume employee view
slides.transcript:
This query consumes the employee performance interface.

The total-sales threshold remains outside the view.

That is useful because different reports may choose different thresholds. The stable performance definition stays shared, while temporary business rules remain report specific.

slides.title: Recent activity view
slides.transcript:
The recent activity view publishes completed transactions from a defined six month window.

That shared definition can support multiple retention analyses.

It creates a smaller, clearer interface than asking every report author to repeat the transaction-status logic.

slides.title: Retention Common Table Expression
slides.transcript:
This retention example begins with the recent activity view.

The first common table expression finds the most recent transaction for each customer. The next stage applies a sixty day inactivity rule.

Why keep that threshold outside the shared view? Because another report may want ninety days instead.

The view owns the stable definition of recent activity. The report owns the temporary business rule.

slides.title: Diagnosis dashboard object
slides.transcript:
The diagnosis dashboard is a good materialized view example.

Its grain and measures are stable. The summary may be read frequently.

And leadership can tolerate a documented refresh interval. The materialized view becomes a small data interface with both a schema contract and a freshness contract.

slides.title: Object catalog
slides.transcript:
An analytics layer should be discoverable.

This query lists views and materialized views in the analytics schema.

Object catalogs help teams understand what reusable interfaces already exist before creating duplicates. They also support documentation and governance.

slides.title: Architecture review questions
slides.transcript:
Before publishing a reusable database object, review more than whether the query runs.

Ask what one row represents. Ask which columns are exposed. Ask how current the data needs to be. Check which source tables and views the object depends on.

[tts-break]

Also ask who owns the business definition and who is responsible for maintaining the object.

These questions turn a saved query into a reliable analytical interface.

slides.title: Recognition checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Use this checkpoint to connect each requirement with the right object.

Temporary logic used inside one statement suggests a common table expression.

Shared logic that should always read current data suggests a standard view.

An expensive reusable summary that can tolerate a refresh delay suggests a materialized view.

A filtered single table view may support controlled updates when that behavior is intentional and tested.

slides.title: Freshness checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Freshness is one of the clearest differences among these tools.

A common table expression reads the source data available to its statement. A standard view reads through to the current underlying data when it is queried.

A materialized view is different. It keeps the stored result from its most recent refresh.

Users should never have to guess which freshness model they are working with.

slides.title: Access checkpoint
slides.transcript:
A limited view can reduce the columns and rows exposed through that interface.

That is useful. But it does not by itself guarantee that users cannot access the base table.

It does not replace grants, row level security, or broader compliance controls. Use precise language about what the view actually protects.

slides.title: Assessment task
slides.transcript:
The assessment has two parts.

First, create the employee and department information view in the analytics schema. The view should include employee name, salary, and department name.

Second, use only that view to calculate the average salary for the Sales department.

The important part is not only getting the syntax right. You should also be able to say that one row in the view represents one employee, and explain why the view is reusable.

slides.title: Assessment reasoning
slides.transcript:
Before looking at a sample solution, explain your design.

The view should have one row per employee. It should expose the columns required for employee and department analysis.

The report query should rely on that interface rather than rebuilding the join. That is how you demonstrate modular design rather than only S Q L syntax.

slides.title: Sample assessment solution
slides.transcript:
This sample creates the employee and department view by joining employees and departments.

Then it queries only that view to calculate the Sales average salary.

Compare it with your own approach. The important points are the interface grain, exposed columns, and reuse of the published object.

slides.title: Module 12 takeaways
slides.transcript:
Here are the main habits to keep from Module 12.

Treat important views as contracts. Keep stable shared logic separate from temporary report logic. Do not assume that every view can be updated.

Be precise about security. A narrower view can reduce exposure, but actual authorization depends on permissions and related controls.

And remember that a materialized view always creates a freshness responsibility. If you store a snapshot, users need to know how and when it is refreshed.

slides.title: Object decision guide
slides.transcript:
Use this guide when choosing a reusable S Q L object.

Use a common table expression for a temporary stage inside one statement.

Use a standard view for shared logic that should stay connected to current source data.

Use a simple updatable view only when write behavior is intentional and tested.

Use a materialized view when storing a reusable result is worth the freshness tradeoff.

And keep frequently changing report thresholds outside stable shared objects whenever possible.

slides.title: Next: Module 13
slides.transcript:
You have now moved from advanced query writing to reusable analytical design.

In this module, you learned how standard views centralize live logic, how materialized views store snapshots, how dependencies affect change management, and why access and freshness need to be part of the design.

[tts-break]

Module 13 takes these same analytical habits into a distributed environment with Spark S Q L and Microsoft Fabric.

The technology changes, but the important questions remain familiar. What does one row represent? Where does the data come from? How current is it? And how can we validate that the output still means what we think it means?
